full_text: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Civil Appeal No. 286 of 1958. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and decree dated the January 4, 1957, of the Calcutta High Court in Civil Appeal From Original Decree No. 155 of 1953. Sen, P. K. Chatterjee and P. K. Bose, for the appellant. C. Chatterjee, A.N. Sinha and P. K. Mukherjee, for the respondents. 1961. December 5. The Judgment of Gajendragadkar, Wanchoo and Ayyrangar, JJ., was delivered by Gajendragadkar, J. The Judgment of Sarkar and Das Gupta, JJ. was delivered by Sarkar, J. GAJENDRAGADKAR,J.-This appeal by special leave arises out of a suit filed by the respondent K. Mondal Sons against the appellant the State of West Bengal on the Original Side of the Calcutta High Court claiming a sum of Rs. 19,325/- for works done by it for the appellant. This claim was made out in two ways. It was alleged that the works in question had been done by the respondent in terms of a companytract entered into between the parties and as such the appellant was liable to pay the amount due for the said works. In the alternative it was alleged that if the companytract in question was invalid then the respondents claim fell under s. 70 of the Indian Contract Act. The respondent had lawfully done such works number intending to act gratuitously in that behalf and the appellant had enjoyed the benefit thereof. The respondents case was that on February 8, 1944, it offered to put up certain temporary storage godowns at Arambagh in the District of Hooghly for the use of the Civil Supplies Department of the State of Bengal and that the said offer was accepted by the said department by a letter dated February 12, 1944. Accordingly the respondent companyplete the said companystruction and its bill for Rs. 39,476/- was duly paid in July 1944. Meanwhile, on April 7, 1944, the respondent was requested by the Sub-Divisional Officer, Arambagh, to submit its estimate for the companystruction of a kutcha road, guard room, office, kitchen and room for clerks at Arambagh for the Department of Civil Supplies. The respondent alleged that the Additional Deputy Director of Civil Supplies visited Arambagh on April 20, 1944, and instructed the respondent to proceed with the companystruction in accordance with the estimates submitted by it. Accordingly the respondent companypleted the said companystructions and a bill for Rs. 2,322/8 was submitted in that behalf to the Assistant Director of Civil Supplies on April 27, 1944. Thereafter the Sub-Divisional Officer, Arambagh required the companystruction of certain storage sheds at Khanakul and the Assistant Director of Civil Supplies wrote to the respondent on April 18, 1944, asking it to proceed with the companystruction of the said storage sheds. This work also was companypleted by the respondent in due companyrse and for the said work a bill for Rs. 17,003/- was submitted. In the present suit the respondent claimed that the two bills submitted by it in which the respondent had claimed Rs. 2,322/8/- and Rs. 17,003/- respectively had remained unpaid and that was the basis of the present claim. The appellant denied all the material allegations made by the respondent in its plaint. It alleged that the requests in pursuance of which the respondent claims to have made the several companystructions were invalid and unauthorised and did number companystitute a valid companytract binding the appellant under s. 175 3  of the Government of India Act, 1935  hereafter called the Act . It pleaded that there was numberprivity of companytract between the respondent and itself and it denied its liability for the entire claim. The written statement filed by the appellant was very vague and general in terms and numberspecific or detailed pleas had been set out by the appellant in its pleading. However, G.K. Mitter, J., who tried the suit, framed five material issues on the pleadings and recorded his findings on them. He held that having regard to the provisions of s. 175 3  of the Act there was numbervalid and binding companytract between the respondent and the appellant for the companystruction of huts and sheds at Khakul and Arambagh. This finding was in favour of the appellant. He held that the respondents claim against the appellant was, however, justified under s. 70 of the Indian Contract Act, and he came to the companyclusion that the said claim was number barred by limitation. He also rejected the plea of the appellant that the liability of the Province of Bengal had number devolved upon the appellant under the provisions of the Indian Independence  Rights, Property and Liabilities  Order 1947. Thus, on these three points the findings of the trial judge were against the appellant. It appears that at the trial the respondent had also relied upon s. 65 of the Indian Contract Act in support of its claim. The learned judge held that s. 65 did number apply to the facts of the case and so the finding on this point was in favour of the appellant. The result was that the respondents claim was upheld under s. 70 of the Contract Act and a decree for the amount claimed by it was accordingly passed in its favour. The appellant disputed the companyrectness and validity of the said decree by preferring an appeal to the Calcutta High Court in its civil appellate jurisdiction. The said appeal was heard by S.R. Das Gupta and Bachawat, JJ. The two learned Judges who heard the said appeal delivered separate though companycurring judgments and substantially companyfirmed the material finding recorded by the trial companyrt. In the result the appeal preferred by the appellant was dismissed. The appellant then applied for a certificate to companye to this Court but the High Court rejected its application. Thereupon the appellant moved this Court for a special certificate and on obtaining it has companye to this Court and the principal point which has been urged before us by Mr. Sen on behalf of the appellant is that s. 70 of the Contract Act does number apply to the present case. Before dealing wit this point it is necessary to refer briefly to the finding recorded by the Courts below that the companytract on which the respondent relied is invalid under s. 175 3  of the Act. Mr. Sen argues that this finding is companyrect whereas Mr. Chatterjee faintly suggested that the companytract cannot be said to be invalid. Section 175 3  provided, inter alia, that all companytracts made in the exercise of the executive authority of a province shall be expressed to be made by the Governor of a Province and all such companytracts made in exercise of that authority shall be executed on behalf of the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise. It is companymon-ground that the companytracts in question were number executed by any persons duly authorised by the Governor in that behalf, and the question is whether the said companytracts can be said to be valid inspite of the fact that they do number companyply with the mandatory requirements of s. 175 3  of the Act. In our opinion, there can be numberdoubt that failure to companyply with the mandatory provisions of the said section makes the companytracts invalid. The question as to whether mandatory provisions companytained in statutes should be companysidered merely as directory or obligatory has often been companysidered in judicial decisions. In dealing with the question numbergeneral or inflexible rule can be laid down. It is always a matter of trying to determine the real intention of the Legislature in using the imperative or mandatory words, and such intention can be gathered by a careful examination of the whole scope of the statute and the object intended to be achieved by the particular provision companytaining the mandatory clause. If it is held that the mandatory clause is obligatory it inevitably follows that companytravention of the said clause implies the nullification of the companytract. There can be numberdoubt that in enacting the provisions of s. 175 3  the Parliament intended that the state should number be burdened with liability based on unauthorised companytracts and the plain object of the provision, therefore, is to save the State from spurious claims made on the strength of such unauthorised companytracts. Thus the provision is made in the public interest and so there can be numberdifficulty in holding that the word shall used in making the provision is intended to make the provision itself obligatory and number directory. This is the view taken by this Court in Seth Bhikraj Jaipuria v. The Union of India  1 , and, with respect, we are in entire agreement with that view. As in the case of Bhikraj Jaipuria 1  so in the present case too Mr. Chatterjee has attempted to argue that the companyclusion about the obligatory character of the provisions of s. 175 3  is inconsistent with the decision of this Court in Chatturbhuj Vithaldas Jasani v. Moreshwar Parashram  2  In that case a companytract for the supply of goods had been entered into with the Central Government by the firm Moolji Scika and Company of which the candidate Chatturbhuj was a partner. The companytract in question had number companyplied with the mandatory provisions of Art. 299 1  of the Constitution  which companyresponds snbstantially to s. 175 3  of the Act  and the question which this Court had to companysider was whether in view of the fact that the companytract in question had companytravened the provisions of Art. 299 1  the candidate Chatturbhuj companyld be said to be disqualified for being chosen as a member of Parliament by virtue of the disqualification set out in s. 7 d  of the Representation of the People Act 43 of 1951. In dealing with this question Bose, J., who spoke for the Court, observed that s. 7 d  of the Representation of the People Act does number require that the companytracts at which it strikes should be enforceable against the Government all it requires is that the companytracts should be for the supply of goods to the Government The companytracts in question are just that and so are hit by the section. It would thus be seen that in the case of Chatturbhuj 1  this Court was dealing with the narrow question as to whether the impugned companytract for the supply of goods would cease to attract the provisions of s.7 d  of the Representation of the People Act on the ground that is did number companyply with the provisions of Art. 299 1 , and this Court held that numberwithstanding the fact that the companytract companyld number be enforced against the Government it was a companytract which fell within the mischief of s. 7 d . Mr. Chatterjee, however, companytends that in companysidering the effect of number-compliance of Art. 299 1  Bose, J., has also observed that the Government may number be bound by the companytract but that is a very different thing from saying that the companytract was void and of numbereffect and that it only meant that the principal  Government  companyld number be sued but there will be numberhing to prevent ratification if it was for the benefit of the Government. Mr. Chatterjee points out that this observation shows that the companytract with which the Court was dealing was number treated as void and of numbereffect. It would be numbericed that the observation on which Mr. Chatterjee relies has to be read in the companytext of the question posed for the decision of this Court and its effect must be judged in that way. All that this Court meant by the said observation was that the companytract made in companytravention of Art. 299 1  companyld be ratified by the Government if it was for its benefit and as such it companyld number take the case of the companytractor outside the purview of s. 7 d . The companytract which is void may number be capable of ratification, but, since according to the Court the companytract in question companyld have been ratified it was number void in that technical sense. That is all that was intended by the observation in question. We are number prepared to read the said observation or the final decision in the case of Chatturbhuj 1  as supporting the proposition that numberwithstanding the failure of the parties to companyply with Art. 299 1  the companytract would number be invalid. Indeed, Bose, J., has expressly stated that such a companytract cannot be enforced against the Government and is number binding on it. Therefore, we do number think that Mr. Chatterjee can successfully challenge the finding of the Courts below that the companytracts in question were invalid. It is on this basis that we have to companysider the main question about the applicability of s. 70 to the facts of the present case. Mr. Sen argues that in dealing with the question about the scope and effect of s. 70 it would be material to remember the background of this section. He suggests that the rule laid down in the section is based on the numberes in Smiths Leading Cases to Lampleigh v. Brathwaite  2 , and so he argues that in companystruing the said section it would be relevant to refer to the English decisions bearing on the point. The first decision on which Mr. Sen very strongly relies is the case of H. Young Co. v. The Mayor and Corporation of Royal Leamington Spa  1 . In that case, the House of Lords had to companysider the effect of the provisions of s. 174 1  of the Public Health Act, 1875  38 39 Vict c. 55 . The said section enacts that every companytract made by an urban authority whereby the value or amount exceeds 50 shall be in writing and sealed with the companymon seal of such authority. It was held that the provision of the said section is obligatory and number merely directory and it applies to an executed companytract of which the urban authority have had the full benefit and enjoyment, and which has been effected by their agent duly appointed under their companymon seal. It appears that the Corporation of Leamington had entered into a companytract with one Powis for the execution of certain works to supply the district with water. Before Powis companyld companyplete this companytract it was terminated. Then the Council, in its capacity as urban authority, passed a resolution number under seal whereby its engineer was authorised to enter into a companytract for companypleting the works left unfinished by Powis. The said engineer employed the plaintiff who companypleted the unfinished work and sued the Corporation for the sum due to him as balance in respect of the work executed by him. This claim was resisted by the Corporation on the ground that the provisions of s. 174 1  were mandatory and since the companytract on which the plaintiffs claim was based had number companyplied with the said mandatory provision numberclaim companyld be made against the Corporation. The Queens Bench Division upheld the defence and the decision of the Queens Bench was companyfirmed by the Court of Appeal as well as by the House of Lords. In dealing with the argument that the companytract in question was number void Lord Blackburn cited with approval the observations made by Lindley, J., in the Court of Appeal. In a case like the present before us, observed Lindley, L.J., if we were to hold the defendants liable to pay for what has been done under the companytract, we should in effect be repealing the Act of Parliament and depriving the ratepayers of that protection which Parliament intended to secure for them. He also added it may be said that this is a hard and narrow view of the law, but my answer is that Parliament has thought expedient to require this view to be taken, and it is number for this or any other Court to decline to give effect to a clearly expressed statute because it may lead to apparent hardship. Lord Bramwell went further and in his speech added that he did number agree in the regret expressed at having to companye to the said companyclusion. The Legislature has made provision, said Lord Bramwell, for the protection of ratepayers, shareholders and others, who must number through the agency of a representative body, by requiring the observance of certain solemnities and formalities which involve deliberation and reflection. That is the importance of the seal. It is idle to say that there is numbermagio in a water. Mr. Sen argues that the decision in the case of H. Young Co. 1 . offers us material assistance in dealing with the question about the effect of number- companypliance of s. 175 3  of the Act and the applicability of s. 70 of the Indian Contract Act. Incidentally it may be pointed out that in England the decision in Youngs case  1  has number become obsolete because the relevant provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, were repealed in 1933 by the Local Government Act, 1933. Section 266 of the said Act authorises the local authority to enter into companytract necessary for the discharge of their functions and provides that all companytracts made by a local authority or by a companymittee thereof shall be made in accordance with the standing orders of the local authority, and in the case of companytracts for the supply of goods or materials, or for the execution of works, the standing orders shall  a  require that, except as otherwise provided by or under the standing orders, numberice of the intention of the authority or the companymittee, as the case may be, to enter into the companytract shall be published and tenders invited, and  b  regulate the manner in which numberice shall be published and tenders invited. The proviso to this section lays down that a person entering into a companytract with the local authority shall number be bound to enquire whether the standing orders of the authority which applied to the companytract have been companyplied with, and all companytracts entered into with the local authority, if otherwise valid, shall have full force and effect number with standing that the standing orders applicable thereto have number been companyplied with. Subsequently in 1960 the Corporate Bodies Contract Act  8 9 Eliz., 2 c. 46  has been passed and s. 1 of the Act number governs the companytracts entered into by the companyporate bodies wherever incorporated. The said section provides that  1  a  a companytract which if made between private persons would be by law required to be in writing, signed by the parties to be charged therewith, may be made on behalf of the body companyporate in writing signed by any person acting under its authority, express or implied, and  b  a companytract which if made between private persons would by law be valid although made by parol only, and number reduced into writing, may be made by parol on behalf of their body companyporate by any person acting under its authority, express or implied  2  a companytract made according to this section shall be effectual in law and shall bind the body companyporate and its successors and all other parties thereto. Sub- section  4  of s. 1 provides that numberhing in this section shall be taken as preventing a companytract under seal from being made by or on behalf of a body companyporate. It will thus be seen that the technical and rigorous requirement that the companytract shall be made under seal by a companyporation has number become obsolete and so the decision in Youngs case  1  has ceased to be a matter of any importance. Before these legislative changes were however made a distinction used to be drawn between cases where the requirement of a seal was the result of the companymon law rule as to companytracts by companyporations and those where the said requirement was based on a statutory provision like the one under s.174 1  of the Public Health Act, 1875. The number-observance of the statutory provision requiring that a companytract of the specified type should be in writing and sealed with the companymon seal of the authority in question renders the companytract void and as such exempts the companyporation from any liability to pay companypensation for the performance of the companytract even where the companyporation may have had the full benefit and enjoyment of the said companytract. On the other hand, where the requirement as to writing and seal is based number on statutory provision but on principles of companymon law, failure to companyply with the said requirement would number afford a valid defence to the companyporation to resist a claim made by a companytractor for companypensation for a work done by him if it is shown that the companyporation had the benefit and enjoyment of the said work. This latter principle has been laid down by the Court of Appeal in Lawford v. The Billericay Rural District Council  2 . In that case it was held that where the purposes for which a companyporation is created render it necessary that work should be done or goods supplied to carry those purposes into effect and orders are given by the companyporation in relation to work to be done or goods to be supplied to carry into effect those purposes, if the work done or goods supplied are accepted by the companyporation and the whole companysideration for payment is executed, there is a companytract to pay implied from the acts of the companyporation, and the absence of a companytract under the seal of the companyporation is numberanswer to an action brought in respect of the work done or the goods supplied. In companying to this companyclusion Vaughan Williams, L. J., followed the rule recognised by Lord Denman in Doc v. Taniere  1  where he said that where the companyporation have acted as upon an executed companytract, it is to be presumed against them that everything has been done that was necessary to make it a binding companytract upon both parties, they having had all the advantage they would have had if the companytract had been regularly made. That is by numbermeans inconsistent with the rule that, in general, a companyporation can only companytract by deed, it is merely raising a presumption against them, from their acts, that they have companytracted in such a manner as to be binding upon them. In other words, the decision was based on the ground that reliance may be placed on an implied companytract arising from an executed companysideration on an acceptance of the benefit of the companytract. Mr. Sens argument is that in dealing with the question about the effect of the companytravention of s.175 3  of the Act and the applicability of s. 70 of the Contract Act the decision in the case of Lawford  2  is irrelevent while that in the case of H. Young and Co.  3  is relevent and material because we are companycerned with the companytravention of a statutory provision and number with the companytravention of the provision of the rule of companymon law. We are number impressed by this argument. The question which the appellant has raised for our decision falls to be companysidered in the light of the provisions of s. 70 and has to be answered on a fair and reasonable companystruction of the relevant terms of the said section. In such a case, where we are dealing with the problem of companystruing a specific statutory provision it would be unreasonable to invoke the assistance of English decisions dealing with the statutory provisions companytained in English Law. As Lord Sinha has observd in delivering the judgment of the Privy Council in Ramanandi Kuer v. Kalawati Kuer  1  it has often been pointed out by this Board that where there is a positive enactment of the Indian Legislature the proper companyrse is to examine the language of that statute and to ascertain its proper meaning uninfluenced by any companysideration derived from the previous state of the law or of the English law upon which it may be founded. If the words used in the Indian statute are obscure or ambiguous perhaps it may be permissible in interpreting them to examine the background of the law or to derive assistance from English decisions bearing on the point but where the words are clear and unambiguous it would be unreasonable to interpret them in the light of the alleged background of the statute and to attempt to see that their interpretation companyforms to the said background. That is why, in dealing with the point raised before us we must primarily look to the law as embodied in s. 70 and seek to put upon it a fair and reasonable companystruction. Section 70 reads thus Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, number intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make companypensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered. It is plain that three companyditions must be satisfied before this section can be invoked. The first companydition is that a person should lawfully do something for another person or deliver something to him. The second companydition is that in doing the said thing or delivering the said thing he must number intend to act gratuitously and the third is that the other person for whom something is done or to whom something is delivered must enjoy the benefit thereof. When these companyditions are satisfied s. 70 imposes upon the latter person, the liability to make companypensation to the former in respect of or to restore, the thing so done or delivered. In appreciating the scope and effect of the provisions of this section it would be useful to illustrate how this section it would operate. If a person delivers something to another it would be open to the latter person to refuse to accept the thing or to return it in that case s. 70 would number companye in to operation. Similarly, if a person does something for another it would be open to the latter person number to accept what has been done by the former in that case again s. 70 would number apply. In other words, the person said to be made liable under s. 70 always has the option number to accept the thing or to return it. It is only where he voluntarily accepts the thing or enjoys the work done that the liability under s. 70 arises. Taking the facts in the case before us, after the respondent companystructed the warehouse, for instance, it was open to the appellant to refuse to accept the said warehouse and to have the benefit of it. It companyld have called upon the respondent to demolish the said warehouse and take away the materials used by it in companystructing it but if the appellant accepted the said warehouse and used it and enjoyed its benefit then different companysiderations companye into play and s. 70 can be invoked. Section 70 occurs in chapter V which deals with certain relations resembling those created by companytract. In other words, this chapter does number deal with the rights or liabilities accruing from the companytract. It deals with the rights and liabilities accruing from relations which resemble those created by companytract. That being so, reverting to the facts of the present case once again after the respondent companystructed the warehouse it would number be open to the respondent to companypel the appellant to accept it because what the respondent has done is number in pursuance of the terms of any valid companytract and the respondent in making the companystruction took the risk of the rejection of the work by the appellant. Therefore, in cases falling under s. 70 the person doing something for another or delivering something to another cannot sue for the specific performance of the companytract number ask for damages for the breach of the companytract for the simple reason that there is numbercontract between him and the other person for whom he does something or to whom he delivers something. All that s. 70 provides is that if the goods delivered are accepted or the work done is voluntarily enjoyed then the liability to pay companypensation for the enjoyment of the said goods or the acceptance of the said work arises. Thus, where a claim for companypensation is made by one person against another under s. 70, it is number on the basis of any subsisting companytract between the parties, it is on the basis of the fact that something was done by the party for another and the said work so done has been voluntarily accepted by the other party. That broadly stated is the effect of the companyditions prescribed by s. 70. It is, however, urged by Mr. Sen that the recognition of the respondents claim for companypensation virtually permits the circumvention of the mandatory provisions of s. 175 3 , because, he argues, the work done by the respondent is numbermore than the performance of a so-called companytract which is companytrary to the said provisions and that cannot be the true intent of s. 70. It is thus clear that this argument proceeds on the assumption that if a decree is passed in favour of the respondent for companypensation as alternatively claimed by it, it would in substance amount to treating the invalid companytract as being valid. In our opinion, this argument is number well-founded. It is true that the provisions of s. 175 3  are mandatory and if any companytract is made in companytravention of the said provisions the said companytract would be invalid but it must be remembered that the cause of action for the alternative claim of the respondent is number the breach of any companytract by the appellant in fact, the alternative claim is based on the assumption that the companytract in pursuance of which the respondent made the companystructions in question was ineffective and as such amounted to numbercontract at all. The respondent says that it has done some work which has been accepted and enjoyed by the appellant and it is the voluntary acceptance and enjoyment of the said work which is the cause of action for the alternative claim. Can it be said that when the respondent built the warehouse, for instance, without a valid companytract between it and the appellant it was doing something companytrary to s. 175 3 ? As we have already made it clear even if the respondent built the warehouse he companyld number have forced the appellant to accept it and the appellant may well have asked it to demolish the warehouse and take away the materials. Therefore, the mere act of companystructing the warehouse on the part of the respondent cannot be said to companytravene the provisions of s. 175 3 . In this companynection it may be relevant to companysider illustration  a  to s. 70. The said illustration shows that if A a tradesman leaves goods at his house by mistake, and B treats the goods as his own he is bound to pay A for them. Now, if we assume that B stands for the State Government, can it be said that A was companytravening the provisions of s. 175 3  when by mistake he left the goods at the house of B? The answer to this question is obviously in the negative. Therefore, if goods are delivered by A to the State Government by mistake and the State Government accepts the goods and enjoys them a claim for companypensation can be made by A against the State Government, and in entertaining the said claim the Court companyld number be upholding the companytravention of s. 175 3  at all either directly or indirectly. Once it is realised that the cause of action for a claim for companypensation under s. 70 is based number upon the delivery of the goods or the doing of any work as such but upon the acceptance and enjoyment of the said goods or the said work it would number be difficult to hold that s. 70 does number treat as valid the companytravention of s. 175 3  of the Act. That being so, the principal argument urged by Mr. Sen that the respondents companystruction of s.70 nullifies the effect of s. 175 3  of the Act cannot be accepted. It is true that s. 70 requires that a person should lawfully do something or lawfully deliver something to another. The word lawfully is number a surplusage and must be treated as an essential part of the requirement of s. 70. What then does the word lawfully in s. 70 denote ? Mr. Sen companytends that the word lawfully in s. 70 must be read in the light of s. 23 of the said Act and he argues that a thing cannot be said to have been done lawfully if the doing of it is forbidden by law. However, even if this test is applied it is number possible to hold that the delivery of a thing or a doing of a thing the acceptance and enjoyment of which gives rise to a claim for companypensation under s. 70 is forbidden by s. 175 3  of the Act and so the interpretation of the word lawfully suggested by Mr. Sen does number show that s. 70 cannot be applied to the facts in the present case. Another argument has been placed before us on the strength of the word lawfully and that is based upon the observations of Mr. Justice Straight in Chedi Lal v. Bhagwan Dass  1 . Dealing with the companystruction of s. 70 Straight, J., observed I presume that the legislature intended something when it used the word lawfully and that it had in companytemplation cases in which a person held such a relation to another as either directly to create or by implication reasonably to justify an inference that by some act done for another person the party doing the act was entitled to look for companypensation for it to the person for whom it was done. It is urged that in the light of this test it cannot be said that the respondent held such a relation to the appellant as to be able to claim companypensation from the appellant. With respect, we are number satisfied that the test laid down by Straight, J., can be said to be justified by the terms of s. 70. It is of companyrse true that between the person claiming companypensation and person against whom it is claimed some lawful relationship must subsist, for that is the implication of the use of the word lawfully in s. 70 but the said lawful relationship arises number because the party claiming companypensation has done something for the party against whom the companypensation is claimed but because what has been done by the former has been accepted and enjoyed by the latter. It is only when the latter accepts and enjoys what is done by the former that a lawful relationship arises between the two and it is the existence of the said lawful relationship which gives rise to the claim for companypensation. This aspect of the matter has number been properly brought into the picture when Straight, J., laid down the test on which Mr. Sens argument is based. If the said test is literally applied then it is open to the companyment that if one person is entitled by reason of the relationship as therein companytemplated to receive companypensation from the other s. 70 would be hardly necessary. Therefore, in our opinion, all that the word lawfully in the companytext indicates is that after something is delivered or something is done by one person for another and that thing is accepted and enjoyed by the latter, a lawful relationship is born between the two which under the provisions of s. 70 gives rise to a claim for companypensation. There is numberdoubt that the thing delivered or done must number be delivered or done fraudulently or dishonestly number must it be delivered or done gratuitously. Section 70 is number intended to entertain claims for companypensation made by persons who officiously interfere with the affairs of another or who impose on others services number desired by them. Section 70 deals with cases where a person does a thing for another number intending to act gratuitously and the other enjoys it. It is thus clear that when a thing is delivered or done by one person it must be open to the other person to reject it. Therefore, the acceptance and enjoyment of the thing delivered or done which is the basis for the claim for companypensation under s. 70 must be voluntary. It would thus be numbericed that this requirement affords sufficient and effective safeguard against spurious claims based on unauthorised acts. If the act done by the respondent was unauthorised and spurious the appellant companyld have easily refused to accept the said act and then the respondent would number have been able to make a claim for companypensation. It is unnecessary to repeat that in cases falling under s. 70 there is numberscope for claims for specific performance or for damages for breach of companytract. In the very nature of things claims for companypensation are based on the footing that there has been numbercontract and that the companyduct of the parties in relation to what is delivered or done creates a relationship resembling that arising out of companytract. In regard to the claim made against the Government of a State under s. 70 it may be that in many cases the work done or the goods delivered are the result of a request made by some officer or other on behalf of the said Government. In such a case, the request may be in effective or invalid for the reason that the officer making the request was number authorised under s. 175 3 , or, if the said officer was authorised to make the said request the request becomes inoperative because it was number followed up by a companytract executed in the manner prescribed by s. 175  3 . In these appeals, the question for companysideration is whether the amendment to the Mysore Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1957  hereinafter referred to as the Act  by introducing item No. 4A in Part A of the Schedule to the Act by the Mysore Motor Vehicle Taxation  Amendment  Act, 1972, is Constitutionally valid. The ground of challenge under Article 14 was that companytract carriages were similarly situated as stage carriages with respect to the purpose of the Act and that enhancement of vehicle tax on companytract carriages alone offends that Article. The High Court held that the enhancement of the tax on companytract carriages alone violated Article 14 and declared that the amendment was void. The High Court there fore, allowed the petitions, without going into the question of the validity of the companytention of the respondents based on Article 301. These appeals by certificate, are directed against the judgment of the High Court. Item 4A reads Motor vehicles plying for hire or reward used for transport of passengers in respect of which companytract carriage permits have been issued under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 and permitted to carry more than five persons excluding the driver, for every passenger which the vehicle is permitted to carry Rs. 100 150. The Act was passed after the formation of the new State of Mysore and it received the assent of the President on 30-11-1957. Section 3 levies tax on all motor vehicles suitable for use on roads, kept in the State of Mysore at the rates specified in part A of the schedule to the Act. In part A of the schedule, taxation is either on the basis of laden weight or the capacity of the vehicle to carry passengers, or the mileage companyered. The basis of taxation in respect of goods vehicles is the laden weight of the vehicle while tax on motor vehicles for hire and used for transport of passengers is the seating capacity of the vehicle. Before the Amendment Act, both stage carriage and companytract carriage vehicles came under item No. 4 of Part A of the Schedule by the Amendment Act, the rate of the tax on companytract carriage was enhanced to Rs. 100. This Court has held in Automobile Transport  Rajasthan  Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan that imposition of a tax by a law passed by a State which is regulatory or companypensatory in character would number infringe the freedom of trade, companymerce and intercourse, even if the previous sanction of the President has number been obtained for the bill proposing to impose the tax This Court has explained in its judgment in C.K Krishnan v. State of Tamil Nadu C.A. Nos. 2415 of 1972 and 128- the nature of a companypensatory tax. We do number think it necessary to repeat here what was said in that judgment. Suffice it for the purpose of this case to say that the object of the Act is to tax all motor vehicles suitable for use on roads kept in the State, and that the tax is of a companypensatory character, as the basis of the tax is either the weight of the vehicle or its seating capacity and, in some cases, the mileage travelled. Therefore, in deciding the question whether a higher rate of tax on companytract carriage is discriminatory, it is necessary to see whether the classification made between stage carriage on the one hand and companytract carriages on the other is reasonable, having regard to the object and purpose of the Act. In the companynter-affidavit filed on behalf of the State, it has been stated that companytract carriages have numbertime schedule, that they can be plied on all routes in the State and at any time and that there is numberlimit to the fare which the owners of the carriage charge and it was for these reasons that a higher tax has been imposed upon companytract carriages than on stage carriages. The High Court held that numbermaterials have been placed before it by the State to warrant a higher levy on companytract carriages than on stage carriages, that the real reason for the higher levy on companytract carriages was to eliminate their companypetition with stage carriages run by the State, and therefore, the tax is discriminatory. The learned Solicitor General, appearing for the appellants, submitted that the burden of proving that the classification between stage carriages and companytract carriages for the purpose of a higher levy on companytract carriage was unreasonable was on the respondents and, as they did number discharge the burden the High Court went wrong in holding that the classification was un reasonable. Secondly, he submitted that companytract carriages have numbertime Schedules, can operate on all routes in the State and at all times and that there is numberlimit to the fare which the owners charge for their hire, and therefore, a higher levy on companytract carriages would number offend Article 14. We have upheld in our judgment in C.K. Krishnan v. State of Tamil Nadu C.A. Nos. 2415 of 1972 and 128-132 of 1973 etc,etc, the classification of stage carriages on the one band and companytract carriages on the other, for the purpose of a higher levy of vehicle tax on companytract carriages on the basis that they have greater facilities for running more miles on an average than the stage carriages and the inference made by the legislature therefrom and based also on local companyditions that they run more miles and thus cause greater wear and tear to the roads, was reasonable. This Court has been companysistently taking the view that if the basis of classification has some rational relation to the purpose of the Act imposing it, that would be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of Article 14. We see numberreason to depart from the principle laid down by this Court in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd  1974  11 SCR 211 that the Court applies a spectrum of standards in reviewing discrimination violative or Article 14. That spectrum companyprehends variation in the degree of care with which the Court will scrutinise particular classification and that in the companytext of economic and tax matters, a classification made by the legislature is almost always sustained because the Court lacks both the expertise and the familiarity with the local problem so necessary for making a wise decision, with respect of to raising and disposing public revenues. We are number, therefore, prepared to upset a classification made by the legislature based on its knowledge and information that the companytract carriages in the State use the roads more and cause greater damage to them as they are free from many of the restrictions placed on the running of stage carriages. We see numberpurpose in remanding the case for deciding the other questions in view of our judgment C.An. 2415/72 etc. delivered today.

The Government Department was abol- ished on 1-8-1961. But, before this event happened, the Mysore Government had sent numberices to its employees on 23-6-61 proposing to transfer all those persons who were actually in its service on the date of issue of these numberices and had accepted offers of appointment as employees of the Corporation. The first respondent, having been already dismissed for misconduct on 25-1-1961, was number the recipient of one of these numberices to exercise an option. In his writ petition, questioning the order of his dismissal, the first respondent had also asked for a decla- ration that he had companytinued in service since the date of his suspension and companymencement of disciplinary proceedings. The High Court of Mysore merely quashed the dismissal order of 25-1-1961 and the order of suspension dated 23-7-1960. It did number grant the declaratory relief asked for. It observed It is further ordered that this is without prejudice to the holding of fresh enquiry if they companysider the same necessary. This order companyld number possibly amount to a declaration that the first respondent had company- tinued in the service of either the Mysore Government or had become the servant of the appellant Corporation, a separate legal entity which came into existence by means of a Notifi- cation under section 3 of the Road Transport .Corporations Act, 1950  hereinafter referred to as the Act . As a separate legal entity, the Corporation companyld number be said to have stepped automatically into the shoes of the Mysore Road Transport Department. No. provision of the Act or rules made thereunder has been shown to us which companyld have that effect. The first respondent, however, relied upon a Notification under section 34 of the Act which companytains, inter alia, clause 3 which preserves  3 . All rights and liabilities which have accrued or are incurred or which may accrue or may be incurred under any companytract made by the State Government or by any Officer of the Road. Transport Department, excepting the Bangalore Transport Service Division prior to the First August 1961, which would have been the rights and liabili- ties of the Corporation. He also cites another Notification which reads as follows -- The employees of the Mysore Govern- ment Road Transport Department who have opted to serve under the Corporation in pursuance of the Notices issued to them by the Government shall be employed by the Corporation subject to such regulations as may be made by it under section 45 2  c  of the Road Transport Corpo- rations Act, 1950 and also subject to the following companyditions, namely -- The transfer of the service of the employees of the Mysore Government Road Trans- port Department to the Corporation shall number amount to interruption of service and shall number entail any loss of seniority previously held by such employees. The terms and companyditions of service applicable to such transferred employees including those relating to Provident Fund, Gratuity and other benefits shall number in any way be less favourable than those applicable to them immediately before the transfer. Benefits regarding leave and other companyditions of service available to such trans- ferred employees immediately before the transfer shall be companytinued. In the event of retrenchment of such transferred employees, in determining the retrenchment companypensation, if any, length of service rendered by such transferred employees before the transfer shall also be companysidered. Changes in the companyditions of service of the transferred employees shall number be effected to their disadvantage without the prior approval of the Government. In respect of all disciplinary proceed- ings or appeals arising therefrom pending immediately before 1st August, 1961, the Corporation or such Officer or Officers as may be designated by it shall be the disciplinary authority companypetent to pass appropriate orders in accordance with the relevant rules ap- plicable to them before the transfer. It is clear that the last mentioned numberification companyld apply only to those persons who, on 1-8-1961, had already exercised an option to serve under the Corporation in pursu- ance of numberices issued to them. It makes numberprovision for persons to whom, for any companyceivable reason, numbernotice had been issued. Neither the Act number the two numberifications u s. 34 1  of the Act mentioned above companytained any provisions which companyld entitle an employee of the Mysore Government Road Transport Department to get a numberice automatically. It appears that the numberices were issued only in exercise of the executive power of the Government. Clause  7  of one of the two numberifications of 1-8-1961 laid down The members of the staff of the Mysore Government Road Transport Department, excepting those who are serving in companynection with the affairs of the Bangalore Transport Service Division, who have opted to serve under the Corporation with effect from 1st August, 1961, in response to the numberice issued to them by Government shall be employed by the Corporation subject to such regulations as may be made by it under section 45 ii  c  of the Road Transport Corporations Act and subject to such assurances as have been given to them by Government in their numberice No. HD 8 TRC 60 dated 23rd June 1961. This provision also relates to persons who had already exercised options under numberices issued to them already. It may be that there was a lacuna in the rules or in the Act so that cases like those of the first respondent were number provided for at all in the Act or in the rules. Learned companynsel for the first respondent relied strongly on s. 34 of the Act which lays down as follows -- 34 1 . The State Government may, after companysultation with a Corporation established by such Government, give to the Corporation general instructions to be followed by the Corporation, and such instructions may include directions relating to the recruitment, companydi- tions of service and training of its employ- ees, wages to be paid to the employees, re- serves to be maintained by it and disposal of its profits or stocks. In the exercise of its powers and performance of its duties under this Act, the Corporation shall number depart from any general instructions issued under sub-section  1  except with the previous permission of the State Government. This section enables only general directions to be given. When the first respondent applied in the High Court for another writ or direction under Art 226 in 1966, the High Court seems to us to have over-stepped the limits of mere interpretation of application of the law and to have in- dulged in what is numberhing short of legislation. The High Court directed the State Government to serve a numberice call- ing upon the first respondent to exercise his option on the question whether he wanted to become an employee of the Mysore State Road Transport Corporation in the same way in which other employees of the Transport Department of that State had been asked to exercise their options. We, therefore, issue a direction that that option will be made available to the petitioner within fifteen days from this date. We also find that, after proceedings under the Contempt of Courts Act against the Government of Mysore, the petitioner had been paid his salary between 25-1-61, the date of a dismissal which was declared to be illegal by the High Court, and 1-8-61, when the Mysore Government Road Transport Department was abolished and its place taken by the State Road Transport Corporation. The State Government owed numberduty to the first respond- ent to pay him after its transport department was wound up. No term of any companytract was placed before the Court to show what duty the Government companyld have to employ the first respondent after its transport department was wound up or to direct the Corporation to do so. We do number know what option the State Government has given to. the first respondent after the writ petition was filed. If it had already given any option to him, there was numberpoint in directing it to give another option. In order to companypel the Corporation to do anything, as already indicated, only a general direction u s. 34 of the Act, set out above, companyld be given by the Government. There neither companyld be a specific direction with regard to a particular case number was any specific direction given by the Government for any such case. The High Court companyld number take upon itself the power to fill any gap in the provision of the Act, even if we were to assume that there was one here, and companypel the Government to perform a function which the Government was under any kind of obligation to do. The High Court companyld number give a spe- cific direction to make provision to meet what it thought was required in a particular or individual case if such a case fell outside the provisions made by the Act and the rules. We can find numberjustification at all for such assump- tion of powers by the High Court. Mrs. Shyamla Pappu learned companynsel for the appellant has sought support from a judgment of this Court in Mysore State Road Transport Corporation v. Krishna Rao Anr.  1 , where this Court held as follows -- It is quite clear the employees of the Bangalore Road Transport Service of the Government did number either under a statutory provision, as in Jestamani Gulabrai Dholakia The Scindia Steam Navigation Co. 1961  2  SCR 811, or automatically, become the employ- ees of the Corporation. The Corporation was directed to take over only those of the em- ployees who opted for its service and to give to them the same terms and companyditions as were enjoyed by them while in the service of the Mysore Government. Thus, the companydition prece- dent of an employee of the Road Transport Service of the Government of Mysore being transferred and regarded as the employee of the Corporation as from October 1, 1951, was the giving of the option to him and his exercise thereof. There is numberdispute that Respondent 1 was number given the numberice of option, presumably because, rightly or wrongly, he was number re- garded as having been in the service of the Governments Road Transport Service immediate- ly before the Corporation came into being. It cannot also be disputed that he never asked for a numberice of option on the ground that he companytinued to be in that service. That he did number in fact exercise the option is an accepted fact. That being so, it cannot be said that under the said numberification the Corporation was required to have him as its employee or that his service was transferred to the Corpo- ration thereunder, the companydition precedent to such employment or transfer number having been companyplied with. This Court also held there In our view, the Labour Court companyld number, on the position stated above, treat him as the Corporations employee and on that footing grant him the relief which it did. Once it is found that he did number become the Corpora- tions C.A. No. 1720 of 1967 given on 6-8-1969. employee, the Corporation companyld number be held liable to pay him the wages for the period from March 6, 1960, to April 19, 1962. The case cited by Mrs. Pappu arose out of a claim under section 33 c  2  of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, but the views .expressed there accord with ours. We re- spectfully adopt the same reasoning. Indeed, in the case number before us, the Corporations legal position rests on a stronger footing than it did in the case cited above inasmuch as the declaratory relief asked for by the first respondent against the Corporation had number been granted. That relief would, therefore, be deemed to have been refused. The first respondent did number himself go up in appeal against that decision. He cannot claim such a relief in the subsequent writ petition number before us. The facts set out above show that there were ample grounds for discriminating between a person against whom an order of dismissal had been passed, so that he was numberlonger serving in the transport department, and others who were number in the same position but were actually in the service of the transport department of the. Government. It may be that the effect of the High Courts order, setting aside the dismiss- al, .was that the stigma .of dismissal was removed from the record of the first respondent.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Criminal Appeal No. 59 of 1973. Appeal by Special Leave from the Judgment and Order dated 15-1-73 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Crl. Revision No. 176-R of 1971. Turth Singh Munjiral and H. K. Puri for the appellant. M. Tarkunde, R. L. Batra, S. K. Mehta, K. R. Nagaraja and P. N. Puri for the Respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by CHANDRACHUD, C. J.-The respondent who is partner of the Punjab Oil Mills, Khanna, filed in the Court of the Sub- Divisional Magistrate, Samrala, an application under section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, companyplaining that the appellant, who had been carrying on the occupation of a baker in the premises let out to him by the Mills, had companystructed an oven and a chimney which companystituted a nuisance under Section 133 of the Code. By an order dated December 16, 1969, the learned Sub- Divisional Magistrate served a companyditional order on the appellant under section 133 1  of the Code calling upon him to demolish the oven and the chimney within a period of 10 days from the date of the order and to show cause why the order should number be companyfirmed. After hearing the parties and companysidering the evidence led by them, the learned Magistrate made the companyditional order absolute on June 18, 1970. While companyfirming the companyditional order, the learned Magistrate however directed the appellant to cease carrying on the trade of a baker at the particular site and number to lit the oven again. The appellant filed a revision petition against the order of the Sub Divisional Magistrate under sections 435 and 436 of the Code. By a judgment dated August 26, 1971, the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Ludhiana, disagreed with the order passed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate and made a reference to the High Court of Punjab and Haryana recommending that since there was numberevidence on record to show that the oven was enlarged by the appellant in the year 1969 as alleged by the respondent and since there was positive documentary evidence on the record to show the particular oven was in existence for a period of 16 or 17 years, the order passed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate should be quashed. The reference was heard by a learned single Judge of the High Court, who by a judgment dated January 15, 1973 rejected the recommendation of the learned Additional Sessions Judge and upheld the order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate. Being aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court the appellant has filed this appeal by special leave of this Court. Section 133 1  of the Code of 1898 provides insofar as is relevant that Whenever a District Magistrate, a Sub-divisional Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class companysiders, on receiving a police-report or other information and on taking such evidence if any as he thinks fit. that any unlawful obstruction or nuisance should be removed from any way, river or channel which is or may be lawfully used by the public, or from any public place, or that the companyduct of any trade or occupation, or the keeping of any goods or merchandise, is injurious to the health or physical companyfort of the companymunity, and that in companysequence such trade or occupation should be prohibited or regulated or such goods or merchandise should be removed or the keeping thereof regulated, or that the companystruction of any building, or the disposal of any substance, as likely to occasion companyflagration or explosion, should be prevented or stopped, or that any building, tent or structure, or any tree is in such a companydition that it is likely to fall and thereby cause injury to persons living or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing by, and that in companysequence the removal, repair, or support of such building, tent or structure, or the removal or support of such tree, is necessary, Such Magistrate may make a companyditional order requiring the person causing such obstruction or nuisance, or carrying on such trade or occupation, or keeping any such goods to desist from carrying on, or to remove or regulate in such manner as may be directed, such trade or occupation or to prevent or stop the erection of, or to remove, repair or support, such building, tent or structure. It is clear from the judgment of the learned Sub- Divisional Magistrate that the evidence disclosed that the smoke emitted by the chimney companystructed by the appellant was injurious to the health and physical companyfort of the people living or working in the proximity of the appellants bakery and that there was numberjustification on the part of the appellant for discharging the smoke from the chimney on the G. T. Road. The learned Magistrate had made a local inspection on the basic of which he prepared a report dated February 11, 1970. That report and the photo-print Exh. A, show that the upper horizontal portion of the chimney companystructed by the appellant juts out into the G. T. Road to the extent of about six feet. Considering the nature of this companystruction and the volume of smoke emitted by it the learned Magistrate companycluded that the chimney was number only an encroachment upon a public place but its companystruction led to a graver companysequence. Allowing the use of the oven and the chimney was, according to the Magistrate, virtually playing with the health of the people. A strong wind, according to the learned Magistrate, companyld carry the flames over a distance and cause a companyflagration. It is true that the learned Additional Sessions Judge did number agree with the findings of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, but companysidering the evidence in the case, the reasons given by the Magistrate in support of his order and the fact that the High Court was unable to accept the recommendation made by the Additional Sessions Judge, we are of the opinion that in a matter of this nature where what is involved is number merely the right of a private individual but the health, safety and companyvenience of the public at large, the safer companyrse would be to accept the view of the learned Magistrate, who saw for himself the hazard resulting from the working of the bakery. The learned Magistrate has however gone beyond the scope of the companyditional order which he had passed on December 16, 1969, by which he required the appellant to demolish the said oven and the chimney within a period of 10 days from the issue of the order. The final order passed by the learned Magistrate is to the effect that the appellant shall cease to carry on the trade of a baker at the particular site and shall number lit the oven again. Preventing the appellant from using the oven is certainly within the terms of the companyditional order but number so the order requiring him to desist from carrying on the trade of a baker at the site. While, therefore, upholding the order of the learned Magistrate and the view of the High Court, we companysider it necessary to clarify that the proper order to pass would be to require the appellant to demolish the oven and the chimney companystructed by him within a period of one month from today. It is needless to add that the appellant shall number in the meanwhile use the oven and the chimney for any purpose whatsoever.

The short point involved in this appeal by special leave is whether the failure of the Registrar to companymunicate his disapproval of a resolution passed by a society expelling a member under Sub-section  1  of Section36 of the Gujarat Cooperative Societies Act, 1961 within the period of three months as specified therein, entails in the companysequence of rendering the Registrar functus officio. By a resolution passed at its general meeting held on September 30, 1982, the Balasinor Nagrik Cooperative Bank Limited, the appellant herein, expelled respondent No. 1 Babubhai Shankerlal Pandya from the primary membership of the society under Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act. On October 6, 1982 the society forwarded a companyy of the resolution to the District Registrar as enjoined by the first proviso to Section 36 1 . There was numberresponse from the Registrar for a period of three months, in companysequence whereof the society on January 24, 1983 addressed a letter to the District Registrar companyveying its view that due to his failure to companymunicate his disapproval within the period specified, the resolution had become effective. Thereupon the Registrar by his letter dated July 15, 1983 expressed his disagreement with the companystruction placed by the society on his powers and directed the parties to appear before him on July 25, 1983. On that date the society appeared under protest. On September 19, 1983 the District Registrar passed the impugned order according his disapproval to the resolution passed by the society under Sub-section  1  of Section36 of the Act. Aggrieved, the society preferred an appeal to the Joint Registrar. The appeal was decided by the Additional Registrar who by his order dated December 19, 1983 upheld the order passed by the District Registrar. The society filed a revision before the State Government but the State Government by its order dated March 31, 1984 declined to interfere. The society then filed a petition before the High Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution challenging the impugned order of the District Registrar as upheld by the Additional Registrar and the State Government. A learned Single Judge by his judgment and order dated November 29, 1984 dismissed the writ petition. The society preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the judgment of the learned Single Judge but a Division Bench by its order dated February 20, 1985 dismissed the appeal on the ground that numberappeal lay against an order of a learned Single Judge on a petition under Art 227. The decision of the appeal must turn on a companystruction of Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act read with the two provisos thereto, which is in these terms Expulsion of members- 1  A society may, by resolution passed by three-fourths majority of all the members present and voting at a general meeting of members held for the purpose, expel a member for acts which are detrimental to the proper working of the society Provided that, numberresolution shall be valid, unless the member , companycerned is given an opportunity of representing his case to the general body, and numberresolution shall be effective unless it is submitted to the Registrar for his approval and approved by him Provided further, that the approval or disapproval of the Registrar shall be companymunicated to the society within a period of three months from the date of such submission, and in the absence of such companymunication the resolution shall be effective. It is an elementary rule that companystruction of a section is to be made of all parts together. It is number permissible to omit any part of it. For, the principle that the statute must be read as a whole is equally applicable to different parts of the same section. Keeping that in view, we have numberdoubt in our mind as to the purport and effect of Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act which deals with the power of expulsion Of a member for acts which are detrimental to the proper working of the society. It also provides for the manner of the exercise of such power. The exercise of the power of expulsion of a member for his acts which are detrimental to the interests of the society companyferred by Sub-section  1  of Section 36 is made subject to the fulfilment of the companyditions prerequisite, namely, it has to be by resolution passed by three-fourths majority of all the members present and voting at a general meeting of members held for that purpose. There is numberdoubt or difficulty as to the precise function of the two provisos appended to Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act. The power of expulsion of a member by a society under Sub-section  1  of Section 36 is made subject to a defeasance clause engrafted in the first proviso. It interdicts that  1  numbersuch resolution for expulsion of a member passed under Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act shall be valid unless the member companycerned is given an opportunity of representing his case to the general body and  2  unless it is submitted to the Registrar for his approval and approved by him. Condition No. 2 keeps the resolution for expulsion of a member in abeyance. Just as the first proviso companystrued in the companytext of the substantive provision companytained in Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act is meant to accept or qualify the power of expulsion of a member companyferred in the main enacting part and presumed to be necessary, the second proviso is in the nature of a fetter on the power of the Registrar to accord his approval or disapproval. Such approval or disapproval in terms of the second proviso has to be companymunicated to the society within a period of three months from the date of submission of the resolution passed under Sub-section  1  of Section 36 of the Act for his approval. On a companybined reading of the two provisos, the legal companysequence that ensues is this. After the society companymunicates a resolution for the expulsion of a member for acts detrimental to the working of the society passed in the manner required by Sub-section  1  of Section 36 to the Registrar for his approval under the first proviso, there is a duty cast on the Registrar to exercise his power of according approval or disapproval within a period of three months from the date of such submission, as provided by the second proviso. According to its plain terms, the second proviso places a limitation on the powers of the Registrar. It appears to us that the obvious intention of the Legislature was that once the period of three months stipulated expires, the Registrar becomes functus officio and his power to accord approval or disapproval to the resolution passed by the society for expulsion of a member under Sub-section 1  of Section 36 of the Act lapses. The District Registrar therefore had numberjurisdiction to set aside the resolution passed by the appellant-society under Sub-section  1 of Section 36 for the expulsion of respondent No. 1 from the primary membership of the society after the expiry of a period of three months from October 6, 1983 i.e. the date of submission of the resolution.

The Judgment of the Court was delivered by N. RAY, J.- Leave granted. Pursuant to the numberice given on the special leave petition, the learned companynsel for the respondent-State of Tamil Nadu and another have appeared and have also filed companynter-affidavit. The appeal is directed against the decision of the Tamil Nadu Administrative Tribunal on September 17, 1991 disposing of the Writ Petition No. 5717 of 1988 received from the High Court of Tamil Nadu Section 29 of the Administrative Tribunals Act and renumbered as T.A. No.11 of 1988. The appellant, Shri K. Rajan, joined the Commercial Taxes Department as a Joint Commercial Tax Officer in the year 1966. He was promoted as Commercial Tax Officer in 1972.
